analysis.one_liner: Treats corporations that reincorporate offshore to avoid U.S. taxes as if they were still domestic companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill closing the corporate inversion loophole cleared the Senate Finance Committee favorably on June 28, 2002 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 without the Senate ever voting on it.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, some U.S. companies technically moved their headquarters to low-tax countries like Bermuda while keeping their real operations, management, and shareholders in the United States. This paper move can cut a company's U.S. tax bill even though little else changes. The bill would treat such companies as domestic corporations for tax purposes, so they could no longer escape U.S. tax by changing their mailing address. It also tightened rules on offshore reinsurance and on transactions between an inverted company and its foreign affiliates.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise shoulder a larger share of federal revenue when profitable corporations reorganize offshore to lower their tax bills. Domestic companies that compete against inverted rivals also benefit from a more level playing field, since the inverted company would no longer gain a tax advantage from the move.

how_it_helps.text: A foreign-incorporated entity is treated as a domestic corporation for tax purposes if it acquired substantially all the properties of a U.S. corporation or partnership, former U.S. shareholders hold at least 80 percent of its stock, and the corporate group has no substantial business activities in its new home country.

For inversion deals completed before the effective date, or where former shareholders hold more than 50 percent but less than 80 percent of the stock, the bill still preserves the U.S. tax base: the company's taxable income cannot be reduced below its 'inversion gain' from the transfer of stock or properties, and tax credits cannot offset the tax on that gain, for ten years.

Companies covered by the backstop rules must file an annual application with the Treasury for an approval agreement on their related-party transactions, and face denial of deductions and disregard of intangible-property transfers and cost-sharing arrangements if they fail to comply; the limit on their deductible interest is tightened to 25 percent of adjusted taxable income.
The bill expands Treasury's authority to reallocate income in reinsurance agreements involving foreign jurisdictions, to take account of the amount of taxable income of each party.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. corporations that have already reincorporated offshore or are planning to, together with their shareholders, who would face higher U.S. taxes on inversion gains and stricter limits on deductions and credits for up to ten years after the move.

drawbacks.text: Approval agreements between covered companies and Treasury on their related-party transactions, and the background information behind them, are treated as confidential return information and exempted from public inspection, so the deals worked out with the IRS would not be visible to the public.

The reported bill contains escape hatches: stock sold in a public offering tied to the acquisition does not count toward the ownership test, and the special rules stop applying if an unrelated, publicly traded U.S. company later acquires the entity, which creates room for deal structures to slip out from under the rules.

Covered companies face a heavy annual compliance burden, including mandatory filings and approval agreements with Treasury, with penalties of lost deductions and disregarded transactions for noncompliance; the bill also leaves untouched the broader U.S. tax rules that create the incentive to shift profits abroad in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a straightforward fix: companies that renounce U.S. incorporation on paper while keeping the same owners and operations would no longer get a U.S. tax break for it. The design carries real concessions — confidential Treasury agreements and carve-outs for later public offerings and buyouts — and it does not address the deeper profit-shifting incentives in the tax code. But the main shortcoming is that it never became law at all, so its provisions were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee approved the bill favorably with an amendment and placed it on the Senate calendar on June 28, 2002, but no senator ever brought it up for a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on April 11, 2002 with bipartisan original cosponsors including Senators Baucus, Dodd, Lieberman, Wellstone, Carper, and McCain, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill: nine of the 49 Senate Democrats and two of the 49 Senate Republicans.

The Finance Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on June 18, 2002, and Senator Baucus reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 28, 2002, with written report No. 107-188.

On June 28, 2002 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 465, and the action history shows no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that had already reincorporated offshore kept the U.S. tax benefits of the move, and no new barrier stopped others from following, because the bill died on the Senate calendar without a vote.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 11, 2002 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and written report No. 107-188 on June 28, 2002.

against.name: Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor schedule and never called S. 2119 up for a vote before the 107th Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. multinationals pursuing offshore reincorporation and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against anti-inversion legislation during the 2002 wave of corporate expatriations, seeking to keep the tax benefits of moving their headquarters offshore on paper.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Senate Republican with bipartisan original cosponsors including six Democrats and John McCain, and its cosponsor list split 9 of 49 Senate Democrats and 2 of 49 Senate Republicans; the Finance Committee chairman, a Democrat, reported it favorably.

industries.industry: U.S. multinationals that inverted or planned to invert
industries.note: These companies had moved their legal headquarters to low-tax countries while keeping operations and shareholders in the U.S., cutting their U.S. tax bills. The bill would tax them as domestic companies and claw back tax on inversion gains for ten years, eliminating the financial reason for the move.

industries.industry: Offshore reinsurance (foreign-domiciled reinsurers of U.S. risks)
industries.note: The bill expands Treasury's power to reallocate income in reinsurance agreements involving foreign jurisdictions based on each party's taxable income, tightening a channel for shifting U.S. insurance income abroad.
